9. This, Mr Neogi submits, constitutes the core consideration that played in the mind of the lower appellate Court in adjudicating upon the validity of the impugned sale deed. Tracing the processes of enquiry before registration, admission and denial of execution, endorsement of particulars, etc as evident in sections 34, 35, 58 and 59 respectively of the Registration Act, 1908 as invariably culminate in the granting of a certificate of registration under section 60(2) of the said Act, Mr Neogi submits that these processes in the very least signify that the ultimate act of certification connotes a process of regularity and raises the necessary presumption of procedure duly followed in effecting the same. That such a presumption may appropriately be made in such cases has been duly endorsed in the case of Gangamoyi Debi vs Troiluckhya Nath Chowdhury reported in 33 Indian Appeals, 60. In Gangamoyi Devi's case it was observed thus at page 65: 

 11. It is in this context that the lower appellate Court had to consider the plea of fraud and collusion. In this Court's view, the test before it was to examine the extent to which there was strong evidence of a deliberate fraud successfully committed to dislodge the presumptions attendant upon registration as so aptly formulated in the Gangamoyi Debi case. Bearing in mind the basic tenet that the law presumes against any illegality and the burden of proof that an illegality has occurred rests on the party who asserts the same mind, and as reflected, for example in the prescriptions of sections 102 and 103 of the Evidence Act, 1872, coupled with the requirement in Order VII, rule 4 of the Code that in any allegation of fraud the pleading should state the constituents of the fraud alleged along with particulars as to dates and items if necessary, Mr Neogi submits that the pleading in this case notably suffered from a lack of specificity in that regard. In this regard, Mr Neogi submits that the raison d'etre of the mandatory requirement of Order VI, rule 4 was explained thus in Swarna Lata vs KIF & M Works Ltd reported in AIR 1974 Calcutta 393 at paragraph 7, page 395 thus: 

 15. In order words, should the words "fraud" and "collusion" be extracted from the plaintiff-petitioner's pleadings in this case, precious little remains thereafter to suggest that there was some wrongdoing on the part of the defendants-opposite parties as was made to unduly prevail upon the plaintiff-petitioner and his choice in action. That is precisely the exercise that the lower appellate Court appears to have undertaken in this regard. The generality and obscurity of the plea of fraud and collusion arising in this case left no scope but for the lower appellate Court to proceed to consider the case by effectively dismembering the words "fraud" and "collusion" from the general body of the plaint and find at the end of the day that, in all probability, and based on documents and evidence available, the acts alleged were, in fact, not tainted with any illegal character and purpose. It is also to be noted that in dealing with a duly registered document the lower appellate Court found itself bound not only by the presumption consequent upon registration, but also by the rules of evidence as debarred the acceptance of any oral statement under section 92 of the Evidence Act for the purpose of either contradicting or subtracting from the terms of a registered document produced in evidence. Indeed, as Mr Saha has submitted, an exception in this regard is to be made in the event that fraud is alleged. But, for the reasons as aforementioned, this court finds that there was no evidence before the lower appellate Court to prove at any level of satisfaction that this was indeed, a case of fraud and collusion to call that exceptional practice into operation.
